newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Missing Pakistani love-match woman reappears.
newsitem.headline: Missing Pakistani love-match woman reappears.

text.p: A 22-year-old Pakistani woman who went missing a few days after winning an 11-month court battle against her father's challenge to her love marriage has reappeared in Rawalpindi, an official said on Sunday.
The spokeswoman for Dar-ul Aman, a state-run women's shelter in Rawalpindi, near Islamabad, said Saima Waheed had arrived on Saturday to be lodged at the shelter under judicial orders.
"Saima is here in Dar-ul Aman since yesterday, but I can't say how long she will stay here," she said.
Newspapers said Saima had sought help from the Assistant Commissioner of Rawalpindi, who used his judicial authority to send her to Dar-ul Aman for her own security.

Saima, who lives in the Punjab provincial capital Lahore, disappeared on Thursday. Her husband Arshad Ahmed, his lawyer Abid Saqi, Saima's lawyer Asma Jahangir and her father Abdul Waheed Ropri had all denied knowledge of her whereabouts.
Her disappearance lent an air of mystery to a case that had symbolised the struggle between Moslem conservatives and women's rights advocates in Pakistan.
On Thursday Saima left a women's shelter in Lahore where she had spent 11 months under a court order.

She said in a statement on Saturday that she had left Saqi's office with Ahmed, who took her to a friend's house initially. Ahmed left to find another sanctuary because he suspected that her family had found out where they were.
"But he did not return for two hours," Saima said. "I got fear-stricken. And I cannot tell how I managed to reach here.
"I am very tired and want reconciliation with my parents. Arshad should try to get the matter settled with my parents so that we could live peacefully," she added.
Saima denied newspaper reports and accusations by her husband that she had developed a romantic liaison with Saqi. "I only know him as a counsel of my husband," her statement said.

On Monday the Lahore High Court upheld Saima's marriage in a 2-1 verdict, ruling it valid in the eyes of Islam even though it occurred against the will of her father, a member of the militant Sunni Moslem Ahle Hadith organisation.
